items.title: In Praise of Unfinished Things
items.tvi: Ca ngợi những điều dang dở
items.text:
There is a particular kind of guilt reserved for the unfinished: the novel abandoned at chapter three, the language course discontinued after a fortnight, the half-painted fence. We are taught, from childhood, that completion is a virtue and quitting a failing of character. Persistence is celebrated in biographies of the eminent; the many projects they quietly dropped along the way rarely merit a mention.
Yet a case can be made that the unfinished deserves rather more respect than it receives. Not every abandoned endeavour represents a lapse of will. Some are discarded precisely because they have served their purpose: the novel that taught its author she preferred essays, the instrument that revealed a love not of playing but of listening. To insist on finishing them regardless is to mistake the form of an activity for its value.
There is, moreover, an economic argument against compulsive completion. Economists speak of the 'sunk cost fallacy' — the tendency to continue investing in something because of what has already been spent, rather than because of what further investment is likely to yield. The reader who ploughs grimly through a tedious book because she has 'already read half' is committing, in miniature, the same error as the government that pours money into a failing project to avoid admitting it was ill-conceived.
None of this is a licence for flightiness. Much that is worthwhile requires enduring long stretches of tedium, and the ability to persevere through them is genuinely valuable. The skill, perhaps, lies in distinguishing between the discomfort that precedes reward and the discomfort that merely prolongs a mistake — a distinction easier to draw in hindsight than at the time, which is precisely why it is so seldom drawn well.

qs.q: What does the writer suggest about biographies of successful people?
qs.a: They ignore the projects those people abandoned
w: They exaggerate how often those people quit
They criticise those people for quitting
qs.why: “the many projects they quietly dropped along the way rarely merit a mention.”

qs.q: According to the writer, why might an abandoned project still be worthwhile?
qs.a: It may have already given the person what they needed
w: It may be finished by someone else
qs.why: “Some are discarded precisely because they have served their purpose.”

qs.q: What links the reader of a tedious book and the government in paragraph 3?
qs.a: Both continue because of what they have already invested
w: Both lack the money to stop
Both are forced to continue by others
qs.why: “the tendency to continue investing in something because of what has already been spent.”

qs.q: Why is the final distinction 'so seldom drawn well'?
qs.a: It is only clear after the event
w: Most people never try to make it
qs.why: “a distinction easier to draw in hindsight than at the time.”

items.title: The Tyranny of Metrics
items.tvi: Sự độc đoán của chỉ số
items.text:
Few ideas in modern management have proved as seductive as the notion that whatever matters can be measured, and whatever is measured can be improved. Hospitals are ranked by waiting times, schools by examination results, researchers by citation counts, and employees by an ever-expanding array of 'key performance indicators'. The appeal is understandable: numbers promise objectivity, accountability and a defence against favouritism.
The difficulty, as the economist Charles Goodhart observed, is that when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. Once people are rewarded or punished according to a number, they inevitably direct their efforts towards the number itself rather than the underlying goal it was meant to reflect. Schools judged on exam pass rates may quietly discourage weaker pupils from sitting exams; hospitals judged on waiting times may reclassify patients to keep the figures down. The metric improves; the reality it was supposed to capture may not.
More insidiously, the activities most easily quantified are not necessarily those of greatest value. The number of patients a doctor sees is simple to count; the quality of reassurance offered to a frightened patient is not. Where only the countable is rewarded, the uncountable tends to wither — not through any deliberate decision, but through the gradual redirection of attention.
None of this amounts to an argument against measurement as such. Data can reveal problems that intuition overlooks, and organisations that refuse to measure anything are hardly models of efficiency. The point is rather that numbers should inform judgement, not replace it. A metric is a tool for asking questions; treated as an answer, it can do considerable harm.

qs.q: Why are numbers attractive to managers, according to the writer?
qs.a: They appear fair and objective
qs.why: “numbers promise objectivity, accountability and a defence against favouritism.”

qs.q: What is the main idea of Goodhart's observation?
qs.a: People focus on the number rather than the real goal
w: Measures become more accurate over time
qs.why: “they inevitably direct their efforts towards the number itself rather than the underlying goal.”

qs.q: Why does the writer use the word 'insidiously'?
qs.a: The harm happens gradually and almost unnoticed
qs.why: “not through any deliberate decision, but through the gradual redirection of attention.”

qs.q: What is the writer's final position?
qs.a: Measurement is useful if it supports judgement
qs.why: “numbers should inform judgement, not replace it.”

items.title: Nostalgia Reconsidered
items.text:
For much of its history, nostalgia was regarded not as a sentiment but as a disease. The term was coined in 1688 by a Swiss medical student to describe the debilitating homesickness of soldiers serving abroad, whose symptoms were thought to include fever, fainting and, in extreme cases, death. Physicians proposed remedies ranging from leeches to threats, and as late as the American Civil War, army doctors were still diagnosing it.
The modern view is altogether more benign. Over the past two decades, psychologists have amassed evidence that nostalgia, far from being a malady, serves a range of protective functions. People who are prompted to recall fond memories subsequently report feeling more socially connected, more optimistic about the future and more convinced that their lives have meaning. Intriguingly, nostalgia appears to be triggered more often by negative states — loneliness, boredom, even cold — as though the mind reaches for the past to warm the present.
This is not to say that nostalgia is without its hazards. Collective nostalgia, in which groups idealise a shared past, can be readily exploited by those seeking to portray the present as a decline from some lost golden age. Such narratives tend to be selective, smoothing over the hardships and injustices of earlier times while magnifying contemporary grievances.
The distinction, researchers suggest, may lie between nostalgia that looks backward in order to sustain us and nostalgia that looks backward in order to reject the present. The first draws on memory as a resource; the second treats it as a refuge. Both are recognisably human, but only one tends to leave us better equipped for the life we actually have.

qs.q: How was nostalgia originally understood?
qs.a: As a medical condition affecting soldiers
qs.why: “was regarded not as a sentiment but as a disease… homesickness of soldiers.”

qs.q: What surprising finding is mentioned about nostalgia?
qs.a: It is often triggered by negative feelings
w: It makes people feel more lonely
qs.why: “nostalgia appears to be triggered more often by negative states — loneliness, boredom, even cold.”

qs.q: What danger of collective nostalgia does the writer describe?
qs.a: It can be used to present the past unrealistically
w: It makes people forget their history
qs.why: “can be readily exploited… Such narratives tend to be selective, smoothing over the hardships.”

qs.q: What is the difference between a 'resource' and a 'refuge' here?
qs.a: Using memories to cope versus hiding from the present
qs.why: “nostalgia that looks backward in order to sustain us and nostalgia that looks backward in order to reject the present.”

items.title: The Craft of Silence in Fiction
items.tvi: Nghệ thuật im lặng trong tiểu thuyết
items.text:
Among the hardest lessons for apprentice novelists is that what a story leaves unsaid can matter more than what it states. Ernest Hemingway famously likened his method to an iceberg: only a fraction of the meaning should appear on the surface, with the remainder implied by what lies beneath. A writer who knows something deeply, he argued, may omit it, and the reader will sense its presence more strongly than if it had been spelled out.
The principle is easier to admire than to apply. Omission, handled clumsily, produces not resonance but confusion; the reader cannot feel the weight of what has been withheld unless the visible part of the story has been shaped to suggest it. A conversation in which two characters discuss the weather while avoiding any mention of a recent bereavement works only if the reader already knows of the death, or can infer it from the strained politeness of their exchange.
Vietnamese literature offers its own tradition of restraint. Classical poetry frequently conveys grief or longing through images of landscape — a solitary crane, an autumn moon — rather than direct statement, trusting the reader to supply the emotion. Contemporary writers such as Nguyen Huy Thiep have been praised for a spare, almost laconic style in which brutal events are recounted in a flat tone that heightens rather than diminishes their impact.
What these approaches share is a form of respect for the reader. To explain everything is, in a sense, to distrust one's audience. To leave room for inference is to invite them into the act of creation — an invitation that, when it succeeds, produces the peculiar intimacy that distinguishes literature from mere information.

qs.q: What does Hemingway's iceberg comparison mean?
qs.a: Most of a story's meaning should be implied, not stated
w: Stories should be cold and unemotional
Only experts can understand good fiction
qs.why: “only a fraction of the meaning should appear on the surface, with the remainder implied.”

qs.q: When does omission fail, according to the writer?
qs.a: When the story does not give enough clues
w: When the story is too short
When characters talk about the weather
qs.why: “the reader cannot feel the weight of what has been withheld unless the visible part… has been shaped to suggest it.”

qs.q: How does classical Vietnamese poetry express emotion?
qs.a: Through images of nature rather than direct words
qs.why: “conveys grief or longing through images of landscape… rather than direct statement.”

qs.q: Why does the writer say explaining everything is a kind of distrust?
qs.a: It assumes readers cannot work things out themselves
w: Writers cannot be sure of their facts
qs.why: “To explain everything is, in a sense, to distrust one's audience.”

items.title: Expertise and Its Discontents
items.tvi: Chuyên gia và những bất mãn
items.text:
It has become commonplace to lament a crisis of trust in expertise. Scientists, economists and medical professionals, the argument runs, are increasingly dismissed by a public that prefers the confident pronouncements of online commentators to the hedged conclusions of those who have devoted their lives to a subject. There is truth in this, but the diagnosis is often incomplete.
Part of the problem lies with the experts themselves. Forecasts confidently issued and spectacularly wrong — of financial stability on the eve of crisis, for instance — have understandably eroded public faith. So, too, has a tendency in some quarters to present contested findings as settled consensus, or to stray from areas of genuine competence into political advocacy while retaining the authority of the laboratory or the university.
There is also a structural difficulty. Genuine expertise is characterised by an awareness of uncertainty: the specialist knows how much remains unknown and qualifies her statements accordingly. Yet public debate rewards certainty. A commentator who declares that a policy will 'definitely' succeed is likely to attract more attention than one who explains that the evidence is mixed, even though the latter is giving a more accurate picture.
Restoring trust, then, may require changes on both sides. Experts might be more candid about the limits of their knowledge and more careful to distinguish evidence from opinion. The public, for its part, might learn to regard expressions of uncertainty not as weakness but as a mark of honesty. Neither change is easy; but the alternative — a debate in which confidence is mistaken for competence — is considerably worse.

qs.q: What does the writer think of the usual explanation for the 'crisis of trust'?
qs.a: It is partly right but leaves things out
w: It exaggerates the role of experts
qs.why: “There is truth in this, but the diagnosis is often incomplete.”

qs.q: Which behaviour by experts has reduced trust?
qs.a: Presenting disputed findings as certain
qs.why: “a tendency… to present contested findings as settled consensus.”

qs.q: What is the 'structural difficulty' described?
qs.a: Honest uncertainty attracts less attention than confidence
qs.why: “public debate rewards certainty.”

qs.q: What does the writer want the public to do?
qs.a: See admissions of uncertainty as honesty
qs.why: “regard expressions of uncertainty not as weakness but as a mark of honesty.”

items.title: The Language of Food
items.text:
Menus are rarely read as literature, yet they repay close attention. Linguists who have analysed thousands of restaurant menus have found that the vocabulary used to describe dishes correlates remarkably closely with their price. Inexpensive establishments tend to rely on vague positive adjectives — 'delicious', 'tasty', 'mouth-watering' — whose very insistence betrays a certain anxiety. Expensive restaurants, by contrast, favour precise, often unadorned detail: the provenance of an ingredient, the name of a farm, a cooking technique stated without embellishment.
The pattern, researchers suggest, reflects different strategies of persuasion. Where quality cannot be taken for granted, it must be asserted; where it can, assertion would seem faintly vulgar, and the restaurant signals confidence through restraint. In one study, every additional letter in the average length of the words describing a dish was associated with a measurable increase in its price — a finding that says less about spelling than about the cultural capital attached to elaborate, often French-derived terminology.
The language of food also carries traces of history. English distinguishes between the animal in the field — cow, pig, sheep — and its meat on the table — beef, pork, mutton — a division usually traced to the Norman conquest, when Anglo-Saxon peasants tended the livestock while their French-speaking lords consumed it. Vietnamese culinary vocabulary, similarly, bears the imprint of contact with Chinese and French cuisine, from 'xì dầu' to 'pa tê'.
To read a menu attentively, then, is to read a compressed account of social class, commerce and history — served, as it were, with a side of persuasion.

qs.q: What kind of language do cheap restaurants tend to use?
qs.a: General words of praise
qs.why: “rely on vague positive adjectives — delicious, tasty, mouth-watering.”

qs.q: Why do expensive restaurants avoid words like 'delicious'?
qs.a: Openly claiming quality would seem unsophisticated
qs.why: “where it can, assertion would seem faintly vulgar, and the restaurant signals confidence through restraint.”

qs.q: What does the writer say the word-length finding really shows?
qs.a: The social prestige of elaborate vocabulary
w: That longer menus cost more to print
qs.why: “says less about spelling than about the cultural capital attached to elaborate… terminology.”

qs.q: How is the 'cow' and 'beef' difference explained?
qs.a: Different social classes spoke different languages
w: Farmers and cooks used different dialects
qs.why: “Anglo-Saxon peasants tended the livestock while their French-speaking lords consumed it.”

items.title: The Paradox of Choice
items.tvi: Nghịch lý của sự lựa chọn
items.text:
It seems self-evident that more choice is better. A shop offering fifty varieties of jam ought to satisfy more customers than one offering five; a pension scheme with a hundred investment options ought to suit more people than one with ten. Yet a body of research, popularised as 'the paradox of choice', suggests that beyond a certain point additional options can leave us less satisfied rather than more.
In a widely cited experiment, shoppers presented with a display of twenty-four jams were more likely to stop and look than those shown only six, but considerably less likely to buy. Faced with abundance, many deferred the decision altogether. Similar effects have been reported in contexts as varied as retirement savings, where larger menus of funds are associated with lower participation, and online dating, where an apparently limitless pool of partners may foster a reluctance to commit to any one of them.
The mechanisms proposed are several. Extensive choice increases the cognitive effort required to decide, and with it the temptation to postpone. It also raises expectations — surely, among so many options, one must be perfect — and multiplies the opportunities for regret, since every choice made implies alternatives forgone.
It should be said that subsequent attempts to replicate the original findings have produced inconsistent results, and the effect appears to depend heavily on context: experts choosing within their own field, for example, seem largely immune. Still, the broader insight endures. Freedom of choice is undoubtedly valuable, but the assumption that its value increases without limit deserves rather more scepticism than it usually receives.

qs.q: What happened in the jam experiment?
qs.a: More shoppers looked at the large display, but fewer bought
w: More shoppers bought from the large display
Shoppers preferred the small display in every way
qs.why: “more likely to stop and look… but considerably less likely to buy.”

qs.q: Why might too many options increase regret?
qs.a: Each choice means giving up many alternatives
qs.why: “every choice made implies alternatives forgone.”

qs.q: What does the writer admit about the research?
qs.a: Later studies have not always produced the same results
w: Experts are most affected by too much choice
qs.why: “subsequent attempts to replicate the original findings have produced inconsistent results.”

qs.q: What is the writer's conclusion?
qs.a: Choice is valuable, but not without limit
qs.why: “the assumption that its value increases without limit deserves rather more scepticism.”

items.title: Monuments and Memory
items.text:
Public monuments occupy a peculiar position in the life of a city. Commissioned to commemorate a particular person or event, they are intended to fix a meaning in bronze or stone for all time. Yet the societies that surround them continue to change, and a statue erected in a spirit of celebration may, a century later, provoke embarrassment, anger or simple indifference.
Recent controversies over the removal of statues in various countries have exposed sharply divergent views of what monuments are for. To some, they are historical documents: to remove them is to erase the past, however uncomfortable, and to deprive future generations of the opportunity to learn from it. To others, this argument confuses history with honour. A statue on a pedestal in a public square, they point out, is not a neutral record but a statement of esteem; history is preserved in archives, museums and textbooks, not in the decision to continue celebrating particular figures.
Between these positions lie a range of compromises. Some cities have added explanatory plaques that place a monument in its historical context; others have relocated contested statues to museums, where they can be displayed alongside critical interpretation. A few have commissioned new works that respond directly to the old, creating a dialogue across time.
What the debate makes clear is that monuments are less about the past than about the present. They tell us not so much what happened as what a community, at a given moment, chooses to honour — and the question of whether that choice still holds is one that each generation is entitled to ask afresh.

qs.q: What problem do public monuments face over time?
qs.a: Society's attitudes change while the monument stays the same
w: They are often damaged by weather
qs.why: “the societies that surround them continue to change, and a statue… may, a century later, provoke embarrassment.”

qs.q: What do people who want to remove statues argue?
qs.a: A statue honours someone, it doesn't simply record history
w: History should not be taught in schools
qs.why: “A statue on a pedestal… is not a neutral record but a statement of esteem.”

qs.q: Which compromise is mentioned?
qs.a: Moving statues to museums with explanations
qs.why: “others have relocated contested statues to museums… alongside critical interpretation.”

qs.q: What is the writer's conclusion about monuments?
qs.a: They reveal present values more than past events
w: They are the best record of history
qs.why: “monuments are less about the past than about the present.”

items.title: The Uses of Doubt
items.tvi: Lợi ích của sự hoài nghi
items.text:
In most professional settings, doubt is something to be concealed. The confident manager, the decisive surgeon, the barrister who never hesitates — these are the figures we are taught to admire, and admitting uncertainty can feel like admitting incompetence. Yet some of the most consequential errors in history have stemmed not from too much doubt but from too little.
Psychologists have long documented the phenomenon of overconfidence: the tendency to overestimate the accuracy of one's own judgements. In studies where participants are asked to give ranges within which they are ninety percent sure a figure lies, the true answer falls outside those ranges far more often than ten percent of the time. Experts are not immune; in some fields, greater experience appears to increase confidence faster than it increases accuracy.
Certain professions have responded by institutionalising doubt. Aviation and, increasingly, medicine use checklists and procedures that oblige even senior practitioners to verify their assumptions. Some organisations conduct 'pre-mortems', in which a team imagines that a project has already failed and works backwards to identify why — an exercise that legitimises the expression of concerns that hierarchy might otherwise suppress.
The aim is not paralysis. A surgeon who doubted every incision could not operate, and a leader incapable of decision would be no leader at all. The skill lies in locating doubt in the right place: before commitment rather than during execution, and directed at one's own reasoning rather than dispersed as general anxiety. Doubt, so understood, is not the opposite of confidence but its necessary companion — the discipline that keeps confidence honest.

qs.q: What does the writer say about historical errors?
qs.a: Many resulted from too little doubt
w: They were usually made by inexperienced people
qs.why: “some of the most consequential errors in history have stemmed not from too much doubt but from too little.”

qs.q: What did the 'ninety percent' studies show?
qs.a: People were more confident than accurate
qs.why: “the true answer falls outside those ranges far more often than ten percent of the time.”

qs.q: What is the purpose of a 'pre-mortem'?
qs.a: To let people voice concerns before problems happen
w: To investigate a project after it fails
To decide who is responsible for failure
qs.why: “legitimises the expression of concerns that hierarchy might otherwise suppress.”

qs.q: How does the writer describe the right kind of doubt?
qs.a: Focused on one's reasoning before deciding
qs.why: “before commitment rather than during execution, and directed at one's own reasoning.”

items.title: Walking the City
items.text:
The nineteenth-century French poet Charles Baudelaire celebrated the flâneur: the idle stroller who wanders the city without purpose, observing its crowds with a detached and curious eye. For Baudelaire, the flâneur was a kind of artist, extracting poetry from the apparently mundane spectacle of urban life. The figure has since become a fixture of literary and cultural criticism, invoked whenever writers wish to describe a particular quality of attention.
It is worth asking, however, who was free to wander in this way. The classic flâneur was male, reasonably affluent and unencumbered by work; a woman walking alone in nineteenth-century Paris risked being taken for a prostitute, and a labourer had neither the time nor the leisure. The supposedly universal experience of the city was, in practice, available to a narrow few.
Contemporary writers have sought to reclaim the practice for a wider constituency. Some have written of the 'flâneuse', the female walker whose movement through the city is itself a quiet assertion of the right to public space. Others have pointed to the ways in which ordinary walking — to work, to market, to school — produces its own forms of knowledge, intimate and unglamorous, about how a city actually functions.
In cities where the car dominates and pavements are an afterthought, the simple act of walking can take on an almost political dimension. To walk is to experience the city at human scale, to notice what speed obscures, and to insist, however implicitly, that streets exist for people rather than merely for traffic. Baudelaire's stroller may have been a privileged figure, but the attention he embodied is available to anyone willing to slow down.

qs.q: How did Baudelaire see the flâneur?
qs.a: As an artist who finds poetry in everyday city life
w: As a lazy person wasting time
As a criminal hiding in crowds
qs.why: “the flâneur was a kind of artist, extracting poetry from the apparently mundane spectacle of urban life.”

qs.q: What criticism does the writer make of the classic flâneur?
qs.a: Only a privileged minority could live that way
w: He did not observe people carefully
qs.why: “The supposedly universal experience of the city was, in practice, available to a narrow few.”

qs.q: What does the 'flâneuse' represent?
qs.a: Women claiming their right to public space
w: A woman who works in the city
qs.why: “the female walker whose movement through the city is itself a quiet assertion of the right to public space.”

qs.q: Why can walking be 'almost political' today?
qs.a: It asserts that streets belong to people, not just traffic
w: Walking is banned in some cities
qs.why: “to insist, however implicitly, that streets exist for people rather than merely for traffic.”

items.title: The Tyranny of Choice
items.tvi: Khi nhiều lựa chọn thành gánh nặng
items.text:
It has become something of an article of faith in affluent societies that choice is an unqualified good. More options, the reasoning goes, mean a better chance of finding precisely what one wants, and the freedom to choose is itself a mark of autonomy. Supermarkets stock dozens of varieties of olive oil; streaming services offer thousands of films; even pension plans arrive with a bewildering menu of funds. Yet a body of research that emerged at the turn of the century has complicated this cheerful picture, suggesting that beyond a certain point, abundance may undermine rather than enhance satisfaction.
The most frequently cited study involved a display of jams in an upmarket grocery store. When shoppers were offered twenty-four varieties, more of them stopped to taste, but far fewer went on to buy than when the selection was limited to six. The researchers interpreted this as evidence of "choice overload": confronted with too many alternatives, people become paralysed, postpone decisions or, having chosen, are tormented by the suspicion that another option would have been better.
It would be convenient if the story ended there, but it does not. Subsequent attempts to replicate the effect have produced inconsistent results, and a large analysis combining dozens of experiments concluded that, on average, the effect of choice overload was close to zero. What appears to matter is context. Overload is more likely when options are difficult to compare, when people have no clear preferences, and when the decision feels consequential. When shoppers know exactly what they want, a large assortment may be helpful rather than harmful.
This more nuanced account has practical implications. Rather than simply reducing the number of options, designers of choices, whether retailers, employers or governments, can make comparison easier by grouping alternatives, highlighting relevant features or offering sensible defaults. The automatic enrolment of employees in pension schemes, with the option to leave, has dramatically increased participation in several countries without restricting anyone's freedom.
The debate also reveals something about the way popular science travels. The jam experiment acquired the status of a parable, retold in books and lectures as if it settled the matter, while the less memorable studies that complicated it received far less attention. A tidy story about the burden of choice proved more appealing than the untidy truth that its effects depend on circumstances. In that sense, the history of the idea is itself a lesson in the dangers of accepting an attractive conclusion without asking how much evidence supports it.

qs.q: What does the phrase “an article of faith” suggest about attitudes to choice?
qs.a: The value of choice is widely accepted without question
w: People are suspicious of having many options
The benefits of choice have been scientifically proven
qs.why: article of faith = niềm tin mặc nhiên, ít ai đặt câu hỏi.

qs.q: What happened in the jam study when twenty-four varieties were offered?
qs.a: More people tasted but fewer bought
w: Fewer people stopped at the display
qs.why: “more of them stopped to taste, but far fewer went on to buy.”

qs.q: What did the large analysis of experiments conclude?
qs.a: On average, choice overload had little or no effect
qs.why: “on average, the effect of choice overload was close to zero.”

qs.q: According to the writer, overload is most likely when
qs.a: options are hard to compare and the decision feels important
w: shoppers already know what they want
there are fewer than six options
qs.why: “when options are difficult to compare, when people have no clear preferences, and when the decision feels consequential.”

qs.q: Why does the writer mention automatic pension enrolment?
qs.a: To show how choices can be designed to help without removing freedom
w: To argue that governments should make decisions for people
To criticise employers for limiting options
To show that people dislike pension schemes
qs.why: “dramatically increased participation… without restricting anyone's freedom.”

qs.q: What point does the writer make in the final paragraph?
qs.a: Simple, appealing conclusions spread more easily than complicated evidence
w: Popular science books are usually reliable
The jam experiment should never have been published
qs.why: “A tidy story… proved more appealing than the untidy truth.”

items.title: In Defence of the Unfinished
items.tvi: Biện hộ cho những điều dang dở
items.text:
Every writer I know has a drawer, real or digital, full of abandoned work: novels that stalled at chapter four, essays that lost their argument halfway through, poems that never found their final line. For most of my career I regarded mine with a kind of low-level shame, as a record of failures I preferred not to examine. Lately I have begun to see it differently.
The culture of productivity in which many of us now work tends to treat unfinished projects as waste. Time management advice urges us to complete what we start, to avoid the guilt of loose ends, and to measure our worth by visible output. There is wisdom in this, up to a point. A writer who never finishes anything is unlikely to sustain a career, and perfectionism can be a sophisticated form of avoidance.
But the logic of completion overlooks the way creative work actually develops. Many of the pieces I eventually published began as fragments of earlier abandoned projects: a character who outlived the novel she was created for, a paragraph that only made sense when transplanted into a different essay years later. The drawer, it turns out, was less a graveyard than a seed bank. What looked like waste was in fact a store of possibilities that needed time, and sometimes a different context, to become useful.
There is also something to be said for the experience of stopping. Abandoning a project is rarely a single decision; more often it is a gradual recognition that the work is not going where one hoped, or that one is no longer the person who began it. Acknowledging that honestly, rather than forcing a conclusion, can be an act of judgement rather than weakness. Some of the most disappointing books I have read bear the marks of authors who finished them out of obligation.
None of this is an argument for never finishing anything. Deadlines exist, editors need manuscripts and readers deserve completed books. It is, rather, a plea for a more generous view of what counts as productive. Not every hour of creative effort will result in a finished object, and the hours that do not are not necessarily wasted. The unfinished piece in the drawer may simply be waiting, as many of mine turned out to be, for the moment when its writer has learned enough to complete it.

qs.q: How did the writer previously feel about their abandoned work?
qs.a: Mildly ashamed and reluctant to look at it
w: Determined to finish all of it
qs.why: “a kind of low-level shame… failures I preferred not to examine.”

qs.q: What does the writer accept about the advice to finish projects?
qs.a: It is partly sensible
qs.why: “There is wisdom in this, up to a point.”

qs.q: What is meant by describing the drawer as “a seed bank”?
qs.a: It contains material that may later grow into finished work
w: It is a place where ideas are destroyed
It holds work that should be sold
It is a collection of other writers' ideas
qs.why: Đối lập “graveyard” (mồ chôn) với “seed bank” (kho hạt giống): mảnh dở dang về sau thành bài hoàn chỉnh.

qs.q: According to the writer, abandoning a project can be
qs.a: a sign of good judgement
w: a decision made in one moment
qs.why: “can be an act of judgement rather than weakness.”

qs.q: Why does the writer mention “disappointing books”?
qs.a: To suggest that forcing a work to completion can lower its quality
w: To show that all published books are good
qs.why: “authors who finished them out of obligation.”

qs.q: What is the writer's main purpose in the final paragraph?
qs.a: To argue for a broader idea of productive work
w: To encourage writers to ignore deadlines
To announce the end of their career
To advise readers to stop reading unfinished books
qs.why: “a plea for a more generous view of what counts as productive.”

items.title: The Ethics of Predicting Crime
items.tvi: Đạo đức của việc dự đoán tội phạm
items.text:
Predictive policing, the use of data and algorithms to anticipate where crimes are likely to occur or who is likely to commit them, has been promoted as a way of making law enforcement both more efficient and more objective. If historical patterns can reveal where burglaries cluster or which streets see repeated violence, the argument runs, limited police resources can be deployed where they will do the most good. And because decisions are guided by numbers rather than hunches, they should be less susceptible to individual prejudice.
The difficulty lies in the data on which such systems depend. Records of crime are not a neutral reflection of where crime happens; they are a record of where crime has been detected and reported. If certain neighbourhoods have historically been patrolled more heavily, more offences will have been recorded there, and an algorithm trained on those records will direct still more officers to the same places. The result can be a feedback loop in which past patterns of enforcement are mistaken for patterns of criminal behaviour, and the appearance of objectivity lends them new authority.
Critics also question systems that assess individuals rather than locations. Tools that assign risk scores to people based on factors such as previous arrests, age or associations may reinforce existing inequalities, and those affected often have no means of understanding, let alone challenging, how their score was calculated. When the logic of a system is hidden, whether for commercial reasons or because of its technical complexity, the principle that people should be able to contest decisions made about them is weakened.
Defenders of the technology respond that human judgement is hardly free of bias either, and that a well-designed system can be audited in ways that an individual officer's intuition cannot. Some police forces have published the methods behind their tools and invited independent review, and a few have abandoned programmes that failed to show clear benefits.
The more fundamental question may be what such systems are for. Prediction can inform prevention as well as enforcement: identifying areas at risk might lead to better street lighting, youth services or support for victims rather than simply more arrests. Whether predictive tools contribute to fairer and safer communities may depend less on the sophistication of their algorithms than on the choices made about how their predictions are used.

qs.q: What two advantages do supporters claim for predictive policing?
qs.a: Better use of resources and less personal bias
w: Better relations with the public and fewer crimes reported
qs.why: Đoạn 1: “deployed where they will do the most good” và “less susceptible to individual prejudice.”

qs.q: Why does the writer say crime records are not “neutral”?
qs.a: They reflect where crime was detected and reported
w: They are too old to be useful
qs.why: “they are a record of where crime has been detected and reported.”

qs.q: What is the “feedback loop” described in paragraph 2?
qs.a: Heavy policing produces data that leads to even more policing in the same areas
w: Criminals learn to avoid predicted areas
qs.why: Nơi tuần tra nhiều → ghi nhận nhiều vụ → thuật toán lại cử thêm người tới đó.

qs.q: What concern is raised about tools that score individuals?
qs.a: People may be unable to understand or challenge their scores
w: They are too expensive for most police forces
qs.why: “those affected often have no means of understanding, let alone challenging, how their score was calculated.”

qs.q: How do defenders of the technology respond to criticism?
qs.a: They argue that algorithms can be checked more easily than human judgement
w: They claim the systems are completely unbiased
They refuse to publish their methods
They say criticism is politically motivated
qs.why: “a well-designed system can be audited in ways that an individual officer's intuition cannot.”

qs.q: What does the writer suggest in the final paragraph?
qs.a: How predictions are used matters more than how advanced the technology is
w: Algorithms will soon replace police officers
Street lighting is more effective than policing
qs.why: “depend less on the sophistication of their algorithms than on the choices made about how their predictions are used.”

items.title: Translating Humour
items.text:
Translators often say that the hardest thing to carry from one language to another is not poetry or legal terminology but a joke. Puns depend on accidents of sound that rarely survive the crossing; references to local politicians or television programmes mean nothing to foreign readers; and the timing of comic dialogue is bound up with the rhythm of a particular language. A line that provokes laughter in Hanoi may produce only polite confusion in London.
Faced with this difficulty, translators adopt a range of strategies, none of them entirely satisfactory. One is to translate literally and add a footnote explaining why the original was funny, an approach that preserves accuracy at the cost of the humour itself, since few things are less amusing than an explained joke. Another is to replace the original joke with a different one that works in the target language, sacrificing fidelity to the words in order to remain faithful to the effect. A third, more cautious option is simply to omit what cannot be translated, quietly smoothing the text into something less playful than its author intended.
Each choice reflects a view about what translation is for. Those who favour substitution argue that a comic novel exists to make its readers laugh, and that a translation which produces no laughter has failed, however accurate it may be. Their opponents worry that substitution gives translators too much licence, turning them into co-authors who impose their own sense of humour on someone else's work. Readers, for their part, are rarely aware of these decisions, and may judge an author as witty or dull on the basis of choices made by someone whose name appears in small print on the title page.
The problem is not only linguistic but cultural. What people find funny is shaped by shared assumptions about status, politeness and taboo, and humour that relies on gently mocking authority, for instance, may read very differently in societies with different attitudes to hierarchy. A skilled translator must therefore judge not only whether a joke can be rendered in another language but whether its target audience will recognise it as a joke at all.
Perhaps for this reason, comic writing is often among the last to be translated, and some of the funniest books in any language remain largely unknown abroad. It is a loss that goes beyond entertainment: humour reveals a great deal about the way a society sees itself, and a culture known to outsiders only through its serious literature is known only in part.

qs.q: Why are puns especially difficult to translate?
qs.a: They rely on similarities of sound in one language
qs.why: “Puns depend on accidents of sound that rarely survive the crossing.”

qs.q: What is the main weakness of adding a footnote?
qs.a: The explanation destroys the humour
w: It makes the book too long
qs.why: “few things are less amusing than an explained joke.”

qs.q: Supporters of substitution believe a translation should be faithful to
qs.a: the effect the original has on readers
qs.why: “sacrificing fidelity to the words in order to remain faithful to the effect.”

qs.q: What do opponents of substitution fear?
qs.a: Translators may impose their own humour on the work
w: Readers will not understand the jokes
qs.why: “turning them into co-authors who impose their own sense of humour.”

qs.q: What point is made about readers in paragraph 3?
qs.a: Their judgement of an author may depend on the translator's choices
w: They usually check the original text
They always know the translator's name
qs.why: “may judge an author as witty or dull on the basis of choices made by someone whose name appears in small print.”

qs.q: According to the writer, why does the limited translation of comic writing matter?
qs.a: Humour shows how a society sees itself
qs.why: “humour reveals a great deal about the way a society sees itself.”

items.title: The Architecture of Memory
items.text:
Cities are full of buildings whose original purpose has long since disappeared: factories turned into galleries, railway stations converted into museums, prisons reborn as hotels. Such transformations are usually celebrated as examples of sustainable development, since reusing an existing structure generally consumes far less energy than demolishing it and building anew. But the question of what to keep and what to replace is rarely only technical or economic. It is also a question about collective memory, and about whose past a city chooses to remember.
Architectural conservation has historically favoured the grand and the beautiful. Palaces, cathedrals and the homes of the wealthy were protected, while the ordinary buildings in which most people lived and worked were demolished with little debate. The result is a selective record of the past, one in which the lives of the majority are largely invisible. In recent decades, some conservationists have argued for a broader approach, seeking to preserve working-class housing, markets and industrial sites as evidence of everyday history.
This expansion has its own complications. Once a neighbourhood is designated as historically significant, property values often rise, and the communities whose history is being preserved may find themselves unable to afford to stay. The physical fabric of the past survives while the people who gave it meaning are displaced, leaving behind what critics describe as a stage set: authentic in appearance, emptied of the life it was meant to commemorate.
There are also buildings associated with painful histories, such as former detention centres or sites of political violence. Some argue that these should be preserved precisely because they are uncomfortable, as a means of ensuring that the events they witnessed are not forgotten. Others, often including those directly affected, may prefer that such places be removed or transformed, so that they no longer dominate the landscape of daily life. There is no formula for resolving such disagreements, and decisions made in one generation may be regretted by the next.
What these debates share is a recognition that buildings are never merely buildings. They shape and are shaped by the stories a society tells about itself. Deciding which structures to preserve is therefore a way of deciding which stories will remain visible, and the most thoughtful approaches to conservation are those that involve the people whose memories are at stake.

qs.q: Why are building conversions often described as sustainable?
qs.a: Reusing a structure usually requires less energy than rebuilding
qs.why: “reusing an existing structure generally consumes far less energy than demolishing it and building anew.”

qs.q: What criticism of traditional conservation does the writer make?
qs.a: It preserved mainly the buildings of the powerful and wealthy
w: It was too expensive for cities
qs.why: “favoured the grand and the beautiful… while the ordinary buildings… were demolished.”

qs.q: What does the phrase “a stage set” suggest?
qs.a: A place that looks authentic but has lost its original community
w: A theatre built in a historic district
A building that is being repaired
qs.why: “authentic in appearance, emptied of the life it was meant to commemorate.”

qs.q: What problem can follow when a neighbourhood is declared historically significant?
qs.a: Rising costs may force original residents to leave
qs.why: “property values often rise… unable to afford to stay.”

qs.q: What does the writer say about sites linked to painful histories?
qs.a: People disagree about whether they should be kept
w: They are usually ignored by conservationists
qs.why: Một bên muốn giữ để không quên; người bị ảnh hưởng có khi muốn xóa bỏ; “There is no formula.”

qs.q: What approach to conservation does the writer appear to favour?
qs.a: One that includes the people whose memories are involved
w: One that preserves every old building
One based mainly on economic value
qs.why: “the most thoughtful approaches… involve the people whose memories are at stake.”
